concept.name: Downside volatility
concept.definition: The dispersion of returns computed only over outcomes below a chosen threshold (zero, the mean, or a minimum acceptable return), isolating the variability investors actually dislike. Its squared form is the lower semivariance, and its target-relative version is the below-target semi-deviation used as the risk denominator of the Sortino ratio.
concept.intuition: Upside surprises are welcome, so counting them as risk overstates danger; downside volatility measures only the harmful half of the distribution.
concept.mechanics: Take the return series, retain deviations below the target T (with above-target deviations set to zero), square and average them, then take the square root. The result, downside deviation, replaces total standard deviation in measures such as the Sortino ratio.
concept.formula: DR = sqrt( E[ (r - T)^2 * 1{r < T} ] ), where r is return, T the target (minimum acceptable) return, and 1{} the indicator function; DR^2 is the target semivariance.
concept.failure_modes: With few below-target observations the estimate is statistically fragile, and results are sensitive to the arbitrary target chosen. It also cannot distinguish frequency from severity: two distributions with equal downside deviation can have very different tail shapes.
concept.misconceptions: Downside volatility is not simply the standard deviation of the negative returns: it is computed against a target across all observations with above-target deviations zeroed, a distinction that materially changes the number.
concept.example: For monthly returns against a 0% target, if squared shortfalls average 0.0009, downside deviation is 3% per month; using it in place of total volatility in a Sortino ratio rescales the risk-adjusted score.
